strengths: SPECTRE addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferable representations for volumetric CT under substantial memory constraints. The local/global transformer hierarchy provides a coherent way to combine detailed crop representations with scan-level report alignment.

The evaluation has meaningful breadth: six biomarker tasks against ten other foundation models, four segmentation datasets, and two report-retrieval benchmarks. Frozen-embedding evaluation helps assess representation usefulness without extensive downstream optimization.

Several results are strong. CT-RATE Recall@10 improves from 5.0% for CT-CLIP to 25.5%, and Figure 3 reports the highest mean biomarker AUC on four of six tasks. Segmentation is competitive with established architectures, even though it does not exceed nnU-Net ResEnc L.

The supplement documents the 229,619-series pretraining corpus, preprocessing, architecture, optimization, and hardware in substantial detail. Explicitly respecting CT-RATE and Merlin training splits and excluding the KiTS23 development fold are positive evaluation practices.
weaknesses: Pretraining/evaluation separation is materially problematic for segmentation. Appendix A includes essentially the full AMOS CT collection in SSL pretraining, while Appendix C evaluates on 300 labeled AMOS scans through cross-validation. Thus, held-out evaluation images appear to have been seen during pretraining. This is unlabeled exposure rather than label leakage, but it changes the interpretation of generalization and comparison with inductively trained baselines. The aggregated AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K sources also require an explicit overlap audit against downstream datasets; none is reported.

The experiments do not isolate the main proposed contributions. There are no controlled comparisons for local/global aggregation, 3D RoPE or its jittering, SigLIP versus CLIP, report rewriting, or pretraining scale. Table 7 primarily studies segmentation optimization and crop size; at the chosen larger crop, SSL and SSL-plus-VLA both achieve 0.871 Dice. Without matched controls, improvements cannot be attributed to the proposed design rather than the larger corpus, model capacity, or text encoder. This matters because most components are adaptations of established methods.

The segmentation comparison does not establish the claimed isolation of encoder quality. Baselines are imported from other papers, while SPECTRE changes preprocessing, optimization, training duration, and architecture. Appendix C also reports five folds for SPECTRE on LiTS but four for the imported baselines. These results demonstrate competitiveness, but small differences cannot confidently be interpreted as representation improvements; a matched randomly initialized SPECTRE baseline is also absent.

Some technical explanations exceed what the formulation establishes. Normalized-coordinate RoPE and fixed anisotropic patches do not explicitly encode physical voxel spacing, and robustness to spacing or field-of-view changes is not directly evaluated. Equation 19 still labels every off-diagonal image–report pair as negative, so replacing softmax with sigmoid does not itself resolve clinically overlapping negatives. Its separately averaged negative term and omitted bias also depart from the usual SigLIP formulation without explanation or validation.

Important implementation ambiguities remain despite the extensive supplement. Section 4.1 describes a masked student but subsequently states that the teacher produces targets from masked views, leaving the actual iBOT procedure unclear. The manuscript does not specify how variable-size scans become exactly 36 VLA windows, and the biomarker experiments omit explicit kNN selection, split, and confidence-interval construction details beyond referring to the benchmark framework.

The broad claim of consistent superiority is not supported uniformly: Merlin substantially exceeds SPECTRE on Findings retrieval, ResEnc L leads on all three shared segmentation datasets, and several biomarker comparisons have overlapping confidence intervals. These are not rejection reasons individually. My weak-reject recommendation instead reflects the combination of evaluation-image exposure, unmatched segmentation comparisons, and insufficient evidence identifying the contribution of the central design choices, despite the promising transfer results.

strengths: SPECTRE addresses a useful problem: learning transferable volumetric CT representations for both localized image analysis and scan–report retrieval. The local/global transformer design provides a sensible way to reduce attention costs while retaining whole-scan context.

The empirical evaluation spans six biomarker tasks, four segmentation datasets, and two retrieval benchmarks. Frozen-embedding comparisons against ten existing models are particularly valuable; Figures 1 and 3 show leading mean performance on four biomarker tasks, with confidence intervals supplied.

CT-RATE retrieval gains are substantial: Recall@5 improves from 2.9% for CT-CLIP to 17.5%, and Recall@100 from 28.8% to 59.9%. Merlin Impressions retrieval also improves at all reported Recall@1 pool sizes.

The supplementary material provides substantial information about the 229,619-series pretraining corpus, preprocessing, architecture, optimization, and downstream evaluation. Segmentation is competitive with strong baselines, and the authors acknowledge limitations on small structures.
weaknesses: Pretraining/evaluation separation is a material concern. Supplement A.1 includes 2,450 AMOS scans, explicitly encompassing labeled and unlabeled data, while C.2 evaluates cross-validation on 300 AMOS scans without describing their exclusion from pretraining. This implies exposure to evaluation images during SSL, although not their labels, and weakens claims of unseen-data generalization. AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K aggregate other public datasets, but no cross-dataset overlap audit is reported. Further overlap cannot be established from the manuscript, yet the evaluation requires this accounting.

The evidence does not isolate the central contributions. Table 7 studies segmentation optimization and crop size, but there are no controlled comparisons for local/global aggregation, 3D RoPE or its jitter, SigLIP versus CLIP, report rewriting, or pretraining scale. At the selected crop size, SSL alone and SSL plus VLA both obtain 0.871 Dice. This does not invalidate the combined model, but leaves claims about the benefits of semantic alignment, geometric design, and scaling inadequately supported. With most components adapted from established methods, these missing controls materially limit the scientific contribution.

Segmentation comparisons do not cleanly isolate encoder quality as claimed. Supplement C.2 changes spacing, optimization, training schedules, and the segmentation architecture, while importing baseline results from other publications. It also reports five folds for SPECTRE on LiTS versus four for the cited baselines. Table 1 calls the results test performance, whereas C.2.5 describes cross-validation validation performance. These discrepancies are especially consequential for small improvements over transformer baselines.

Several technical explanations exceed what the formulation establishes. Fixed anisotropic patches and normalized-coordinate RoPE do not explicitly encode each scan's physical voxel spacing; preprocessing instead resamples to fixed spacing. No robustness experiment validates the stronger geometry claims. Likewise, Equation 19 still labels every off-diagonal image–text pair as negative, so replacing softmax with sigmoid does not itself resolve clinically overlapping negatives. Section 4.1 also ambiguously states that the teacher receives masked views, leaving an important implementation detail unclear.

The headline claim of consistent superiority needs qualification. SPECTRE trails Merlin substantially on Findings retrieval, including Recall@1 of 33.0% versus 59.4% at N=128, and trails nnU-Net ResEnc L on all three datasets where that baseline is reported. These are acceptable limitations for a broadly useful model, but they contradict the strongest framing. Overall, the worthwhile transfer and retrieval results are outweighed by unresolved evaluation separation and insufficient evidence attributing improvements to the proposed design, supporting weak rejection.

strengths: SPECTRE addresses a valuable problem: learning transferable volumetric CT representations from public datasets. The local/global transformer hierarchy provides a practical way to combine detailed regional features with scan-level report alignment, and the 229,619-series pretraining corpus is a substantial contribution in scale.

Evaluation covers complementary capabilities: six frozen-feature biomarker tasks, four segmentation datasets, and two report-retrieval benchmarks. Figure 3 shows particularly strong lung-nodule classification performance, with confidence intervals provided rather than only point estimates.

The CT-RATE retrieval improvement is substantial: Recall@5 increases from 2.9% for CT-CLIP to 17.5%, and Recall@100 from 28.8% to 59.9%. SPECTRE also improves Merlin Impressions Recall@1 across all three reported pool sizes. These results support useful clinical text–image alignment.

The encoder-only segmentation adaptation achieves competitive performance without an elaborate decoder, including 86.64 Dice on KiTS23 and 80.14 on LiTS. The supplement supplies considerable detail about preprocessing, model dimensions, optimization, hardware, and downstream adaptation.
weaknesses: Pretraining/evaluation separation is a material concern. Appendix A.1 includes the labeled AMOS CT collection in SSL pretraining, while Appendix C.2 evaluates cross-validation on 300 AMOS volumes without describing exclusion from pretraining. Thus, held-out segmentation images appear to have been seen during SSL. This is not label leakage, but it changes the experiment into a transductive setting and weakens comparisons with models lacking that exposure. AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K also aggregate existing public datasets, yet no cross-dataset patient/scan overlap audit is reported. The explicit CT-RATE and Merlin training-split restrictions are good, but do not resolve these other overlaps.

The experiments do not isolate the central methodological contributions. Table 7 mainly studies segmentation optimization and crop size; it contains no from-scratch baseline and finds identical Dice of 0.871 for SSL-only and SSL-plus-VLA initialization at the selected crop size. There are no controlled evaluations of the local/global hierarchy, geometry encoding, SigLIP versus CLIP, report paraphrasing, or data/model scaling. Consequently, the results establish a capable integrated system but do not establish which proposed adaptations are responsible, especially given simultaneous changes in training data, model capacity, and text encoder.

Segmentation comparisons do not fully support the claim that gains isolate encoder representation quality. Baselines are imported from different publications, SPECTRE changes preprocessing and optimization, and the supplement specifies five-fold LiTS results for SPECTRE versus four-fold results for cited baselines. Several transformer improvements are small, such as 83.31 versus 83.19 on WORD, without uncertainty estimates. Competitive segmentation is supported; tightly controlled superiority is not.

Some central technical claims exceed the described mechanism. RoPE uses normalized coordinates and global scale jitter after fixed-spacing resampling; explicit acquisition-specific voxel spacing is not shown entering the positional encoding, and robustness to anisotropy or field-of-view changes is not directly tested. Likewise, Equation 19 still labels every off-diagonal image–text pair negative, so the claimed accommodation of many-to-many clinical semantics is not established. The iBOT description also says the teacher receives masked views, leaving an important ambiguity relative to the usual unmasked-teacher formulation.

The abstract's consistent-outperformance claim is too broad: Merlin substantially outperforms SPECTRE on Findings retrieval, and convolutional segmentation baselines remain stronger. Reproducibility also remains incomplete: the supplied code footnote has no URL, and details such as the fixed 36-window full-scan coverage are insufficiently specified. Overall, the useful transfer results are outweighed by unresolved evaluation overlap and insufficient evidence for the paper's principal architectural and training claims, leading to a weak reject.

strengths: SPECTRE presents a useful integration of volumetric local/global transformers, self-distillation, and report alignment. Summarizing local windows before global attention provides a practical architecture for processing large CT volumes.

The evaluation spans frozen biomarker classification, fine-tuned segmentation, and report-to-scan retrieval. Figure 3 reports the highest mean AUC on four of six biomarker tasks against ten existing models, with particularly convincing gains on LUNA16 and DLCS.

CT-RATE retrieval improves substantially over CT-CLIP: Recall@5 increases from 2.9% to 17.5%, and Recall@100 from 28.8% to 59.9%. Respecting the original CT-RATE and Merlin training splits supports these held-out retrieval comparisons.

Segmentation results demonstrate useful dense representations without an elaborate decoder. The supplementary decoder and training-budget experiments meaningfully examine limitations, including poor small-lesion sensitivity, rather than reporting only favorable aggregate results.

The supplement documents dataset composition, preprocessing, architecture, optimization, and hardware. Building on publicly available datasets offers a potentially valuable foundation for reproducible CT representation research.
weaknesses: Pretraining/evaluation independence is insufficiently established across the full benchmark suite. Appendix A includes aggregated public datasets such as AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K, but provides no source-level or patient-level overlap audit against the downstream datasets. Excluding AMOS explicitly is helpful, but does not resolve possible overlap through these aggregated collections. This is an unresolved validity concern, not evidence that leakage occurred.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the central methodological claims. There are no controlled comparisons for local/global aggregation, RoPE jitter, SigLIP versus CLIP, report rewriting, or pretraining scale. Table 8 compares SSL and SSL-plus-VLA for one segmentation development fold, with identical Dice at the final crop size, but does not establish their respective contributions to biomarker prediction or retrieval. Consequently, improvements cannot be attributed confidently to the proposed adaptations rather than data volume, model capacity, or the text encoder.

Segmentation comparisons are less controlled than the main text suggests. Appendix C.2.5 imports baseline results from prior work; LiTS baselines exclude their development fold whereas SPECTRE reports five folds. SPECTRE also changes preprocessing and optimization. Its margins over Primus-L are only 0.60, 0.24, and 0.32 Dice points on KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD, without uncertainty estimates. These results support competitiveness more clearly than superiority attributable specifically to encoder quality.

Several broad claims exceed the evidence. Merlin substantially outperforms SPECTRE on Findings retrieval, including Recall@1 of 59.4% versus 33.0% at N=128. Table 10 reports only 1.53% small-mass detection for SEoMT at the standard training budget, making the limitation more consequential than slightly smoothed boundaries. Strong overall performance does not establish uniformly strong clinical or fine-grained transfer.

The geometry and alignment explanations need technical qualification. Normalized-coordinate RoPE and fixed anisotropic patches do not explicitly encode each scan's physical voxel spacing; one native-spacing retrieval experiment supports limited robustness, not general geometric consistency. Equation 19 still labels every unmatched report as negative, so sigmoid loss alone does not resolve overlapping clinical semantics. Its negative normalization and omitted bias also differ from standard SigLIP, without an ablation explaining these choices.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial supplementary detail: the code links are blank, the iBOT description ambiguously states that teacher inputs are masked, and the construction of the fixed 36-window scan representation is underspecified. Overall, the strong empirical utility places this near acceptance, but unresolved evaluation independence and weak attribution of the central technical contributions keep my recommendation borderline.

strengths: SPECTRE provides a useful integration of local/global volumetric transformers, self-distillation, and report alignment, trained on 229,619 publicly accessible CT series. Its contribution is primarily a practical representation-learning framework with broad downstream applicability.

The frozen-embedding evaluation compares 11 foundation models across six biomarker tasks using an established benchmark. SPECTRE leads on four tasks, with particularly convincing improvements on LUNA16 and DLCS; Figure 3 also provides confidence intervals.

Cross-modal retrieval shows substantial gains on CT-RATE: Recall@5 increases from 2.9% to 17.5%, and Recall@100 from 28.8% to 59.9%. Improvements on Merlin Impressions provide additional evidence that the learned alignment is useful.

Segmentation evaluation is reasonably broad, including three organ/tumor datasets and additional TotalSegmentator benchmarks. The supplement includes meaningful decoder, optimization, crop-size, and small-lesion analyses, and documents preprocessing, training hyperparameters, and hardware.
weaknesses: The central methodological claims are insufficiently isolated. There are no controlled comparisons for local/global aggregation, positional jitter, SigLIP versus CLIP, or report rewriting, and no data/model scaling experiments despite the emphasis on scaling. Table 8 compares SSL with SSL+VLA only for one segmentation fold; at the selected crop size both obtain 0.871 Dice. Thus the evidence establishes a capable combined system but does not determine which proposed choices produce its gains.

Pretraining–evaluation separation is incompletely documented. Appendix A includes AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K, explicitly described as aggregations of existing public datasets, without tracing their constituent cases against downstream benchmarks or reporting cross-source deduplication. Excluding AMOS alone does not establish independence for the remaining abdominal evaluations. This is an unresolved contamination risk, rather than demonstrated leakage, but materially affects the generalization claims.

The segmentation comparison does not isolate encoder quality as claimed. Baseline results are imported from prior work, while SPECTRE uses different optimization, preprocessing, and training budgets. Appendix C.2.5 also indicates four-fold baseline results on LiTS, whereas SPECTRE reports five folds. Table 10 demonstrates that decoder choice itself substantially affects performance. These results support practical competitiveness, but not clean causal attribution to the pretrained encoder.

Geometry and objective descriptions require technical clarification. Normalized coordinates, a fixed anisotropic patch shape, and isotropic coordinate jitter do not explicitly encode each scan's physical voxel spacing as the introduction suggests. The native-spacing retrieval check is encouraging but limited. Equation 19 separately averages negative pairs and omits the usual SigLIP bias, while Equation 20 averages two mathematically identical all-pairs sums. Section 4.1 also describes masked teacher inputs, leaving an important departure from standard iBOT targets unclear.

Several conclusions overstate the results. Merlin is substantially stronger on Findings retrieval, and nnU-Net ResEnc L exceeds SPECTRE on all three main segmentation datasets. More consequentially, Table 10 reports only 1.53% detection of sub-10-mm masses for SEoMT at the standard training budget, a stronger limitation than mildly smoothed predictions. The small-lesion sample size, detection criterion, and unusually small Dice values need clarification.

Reproducibility is helped by the detailed supplement but remains incomplete: code links are blank, full-scan cropping/padding into 36 windows is not specified, and exact biomarker scores are presented graphically. Overall, the substantial transfer and retrieval results balance meaningful concerns about evaluation independence and attribution, placing the manuscript near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: SPECTRE addresses a useful computer vision problem: learning transferable volumetric CT representations under substantial memory and supervision constraints. Its local/global transformer architecture and sequential self-supervised and report-alignment training form a coherent, practical system.

The evaluation covers complementary capabilities: six frozen-feature biomarker benchmarks, multiple segmentation datasets, and CT–report retrieval. Figure 3 reports confidence intervals and supports particularly strong results on LUNA16 and DLCS against a broad set of CT foundation models.

The CT-RATE retrieval improvement is substantial: Recall@5 increases from 2.9% for CT-CLIP to 17.5%, and Recall@100 from 28.8% to 59.9%. Merlin Impressions retrieval also improves at Recall@1 across all three pool sizes.

Segmentation results demonstrate useful dense representations without an elaborate decoder. SPECTRE exceeds the listed transformer baselines on KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD, although stronger convolutional baselines remain ahead. The supplementary decoder and small-lesion analyses provide valuable evidence about the approach’s limitations.

Pretraining uses publicly available datasets, and the supplement documents corpus composition, preprocessing, architecture, training schedules, and hardware. Respecting the original CT-RATE and Merlin training splits is a positive aspect of the retrieval evaluation.
weaknesses: The main methodological claims are insufficiently isolated. There are no controlled comparisons for local/global aggregation, positional jitter, SigLIP versus CLIP, report rewriting, or pretraining scale. Table 8 compares SSL with SSL+VLA only for segmentation and shows identical Dice at the selected crop size. Consequently, the study establishes a capable combined system more convincingly than it establishes which proposed adaptations are responsible for its gains.

Pretraining/evaluation separation is incompletely established for the aggregated abdominal datasets. Appendix A explicitly describes AbdomenAtlas and AbdomenCT-1K as collections assembled from existing public datasets, but supplies no source-level or patient-level overlap audit against the downstream benchmarks. Excluding AMOS alone does not resolve this concern. This is an uncertainty about the independence of the transfer evidence, rather than proof of contamination.

Segmentation comparisons do not fully support the claim that gains isolate encoder representation quality. SPECTRE changes preprocessing, optimization, training duration, and the prediction architecture; several baseline results are imported from prior work. Appendix C.2.5 also describes four-fold LiTS baseline averages while SPECTRE apparently uses five folds. The small advantages over Primus therefore need more cautious interpretation, especially without segmentation uncertainty estimates or a matched randomly initialized SPECTRE baseline.

Some central technical explanations overstate what the formulation provides. Normalized-coordinate RoPE and fixed anisotropic patches do not explicitly encode each scan’s physical voxel spacing. Likewise, Equation 19 still treats every off-diagonal image–report pair as negative, so sigmoid loss alone does not resolve clinically overlapping negatives. The masked-teacher description for iBOT also leaves unclear whether targets actually follow the standard unmasked-teacher implementation.

The broad claim of consistent superiority is not supported across settings. Merlin substantially outperforms SPECTRE on Findings retrieval—for example, Recall@1 is 59.4% versus 33.0% at pool size 128—and nnU-Net ResEnc L wins all three main segmentation benchmarks. Table 10 additionally shows only 1.53% small-mass detection for SEoMT at 37.5k steps, a considerably stronger limitation than slightly smoothed boundaries.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful implementation detail. The manuscript’s code links are blank, the exact selection and arrangement of 36 windows for variable-size scans are unclear, and the biomarker evaluation does not specify its kNN selection and split details directly. Efficiency is motivated analytically but not quantified with runtime, memory, or training-cost comparisons.

Overall, the broad transfer evidence and large CT-RATE retrieval gains make this a worthwhile contribution. However, unresolved evaluation independence and comparison issues, together with weak attribution of the central design claims, place the submitted evidence near the acceptance boundary. These concerns determine the borderline rating; failure to beat every benchmark does not.
